claims.text: A hybrid machine-learning interatomic-potential and targeted ab initio correction workflow can accurately evaluate the free energies of both solid and liquid phases at fusion conditions.
The hybrid workflow will substantially reduce computational cost relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
The workflow will remain effective in multicomponent high-entropy systems.
A limited ab initio training dataset is sufficient to train machine-learning potentials for rapid phase-space sampling.
Periodic localized ab initio corrections can account for vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The proposed method applies near fusion, approximately from 0.8 to 1.2 times the melting temperature.
The proposed method is intended for systems containing up to approximately five or six components.
A machine-learned potential can accurately map the relevant free-energy landscape.
Sparse ab initio corrections retain detailed anharmonic and electron–vibration contributions.
Machine-learning potentials drastically accelerate phase-space sampling.
Inserted ab initio free-energy corrections ensure accurate treatment of anharmonic vibrational entropy and electron–vibration interactions.
The hybrid method can reconstruct complete solid and liquid free-energy surfaces using a fraction of the resources required by full ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD.
The workflow will provide at least a fivefold computational speedup over explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
The workflow will predict free-energy differences and fusion temperatures within a few percent of full ab initio molecular-dynamics evaluations.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations and TOR-TILD become prohibitively expensive for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The method is most effective when anharmonicity can be corrected reliably with sparse ab initio sampling.
Accuracy may diminish under exceptionally strong anharmonicity or when chemical complexity exceeds the machine-learning model's training domain.
The exact speedup, fidelity limit, and minimum required frequency of ab initio corrections remain unknown.
The workflow can be benchmarked against explicit ab initio molecular dynamics using solid–liquid free-energy differences, melting temperature, percentage error, and total computational time.

contradictions.description: The predicted fidelity is stated as within a few percent, but the falsification rule describes an acceptable error margin with the example '>5% deviation.' Greater than 5% would ordinarily represent failure rather than an acceptable margin, making the threshold direction internally inconsistent.
